article_title: Every Classroom, Every Day (ECED) — Reading
citation: Every Classroom, Every Day (ECED). (2019). Evidence for ESSA program review. https://www.evidenceforessa.org
title: ECED professional development model: institute, site visits, and monthly check-ins across two years
description: ECED's professional development combines an initial institute, recurring on-site visits, and regular remote check-ins. Four 3-day site visits per year
Monthly phone check-ins
constraints: The second year of professional development is optional, but recommended

article_title: ECNUClaw: A Learner-Profiled Intelligent Study Companion Framework for K-12 Personalized Education
citation: Yizhou Zhou, Jiayin Li, and Zhi Zhang. (2026). ECNUClaw: A Learner-Profiled Intelligent Study Companion Framework for K-12 Personalized Education. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.08040
title: ECNUClaw: an open-source Python framework for learner-profiled intelligent study companions in K-12 education
description: ECNUClaw is an open-source framework for building learner-profiled intelligent study companions in K-12 education. It implements "a five-dimension learner profile—covering cognitive, behavioral, emotional, metacognitive, and contextual dimensions" extracted at each dialogue turn, and feeds profile updates into an adaptive strategy engine. The framework is implemented in Python, supports seven Chinese LLM providers through an OpenAI-compatible adapter layer, and its source code is publicly released on GitHub.
requirements: Requires a Python 3.9+ environment with an OpenAI-compatible LLM provider configured through the setup wizard
constraints: The authors describe it as "a framework for building learner-profiled study companions, not a finished product"; the CLI-only interface limits accessibility for younger students
target_learners: K-12 students
target_learning_goals: Subject learning across math, Chinese, science, writing, and reading, with emotional and metacognitive support
examples: The system comprises 25 Python modules across five packages and is tested by 67 unit tests covering agent lifecycle, intent routing, tool execution, memory operations, and learner profile updates
key_sources: Yizhou Zhou, Jiayin Li, and Zhi Zhang. (2026). ECNUClaw: A Learner-Profiled Intelligent Study Companion Framework for K-12 Personalized Education. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.08040

article_title: Once a Response, Always a Response: Detecting LLM-generated Text via Latent Prompt Restoration
citation: Hongrui Bao, Yubing Ren, Jinhan You, Fang Fang, Shi Wang, Yanan Cao. (2026). ONCE A RESPONSE, ALWAYS A RESPONSE: DETECTING LLM-GENERATED TEXT VIA LATENT PROMPT RESTORATION. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05741
title: EchoPrompt: a training-free zero-shot detector using restored assistant-context calibrated scoring
description: EchoPrompt is a three-step training-free detector: it (1) prepends a unified task-agnostic assistant-style prefix to restore a generic response context, (2) computes token-level log-likelihoods under an instruction-tuned proxy model on the restored sequence and under the base model on the original text, defining a context-calibrated token-level gap averaged into a sequence score, and (3) applies threshold-based detection where a higher score indicates stronger latent prompt dependency. Its score is Score_EchoPrompt(X; cg) = (1/(n-1)) * sum of log P_inst(xt|cg,x<t) - log P_base(xt|x<t).
requirements: an instruction-tuned proxy model paired with its corresponding base model
a fixed generic assistant-style prefix, selected on an independent HC3 development set and fixed across datasets and proxy families
a decision threshold
constraints: non-chat/completion outputs yield lower AUROC (82.50% on RAID)
it may produce false positives and false negatives; the authors do not recommend it as definitive evidence of authorship or the sole basis for consequential decisions
target_learners: researchers
platform moderators
educators screening LLM-generated text
target_learning_goals: zero-shot detection of machine-generated text
examples: Runtime per sample is 0.254s, a middle-range efficiency relative to heavier baselines like LastDE++ (1.529s) and DNA-DetectLLM (0.444s)
key_sources: Hongrui Bao, Yubing Ren, Jinhan You, Fang Fang, Shi Wang, Yanan Cao. (2026). ONCE A RESPONSE, ALWAYS A RESPONSE: DETECTING LLM-GENERATED TEXT VIA LATENT PROMPT RESTORATION. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05741

article_title: Expert Cognition Dashboard: From Learning Analytics to Cognition Intelligence in AI-Driven Education
citation: Yuan, A. (2026). Expert Cognition Dashboard: From Learning Analytics to Cognition Intelligence in AI-Driven Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.17263
title: Expert Cognition Dashboard as cognitive middleware between learner behaviours and AI-driven expert reasoning
description: The ECD is defined as "a cognition-centred infrastructure that transforms learner behaviours into interpretable cognitive structures for AI-driven expert reasoning, adaptive intervention, and multi-level educational interpretation." Rather than a visualisation endpoint, the dashboard is an intermediate cognition layer that transforms fragmented behavioural signals into coherent cognition structures, enables multi-level aggregation, and provides interpretability for AI reasoning. The article argues dashboards become "perception infrastructures through which AI systems understand learners."
requirements: AI Tutor analysis to interpret learner behaviours before dashboard aggregation
constraints: The article states ECD is not intended to fully capture or automate expert judgment, and is not intended to replace human educators
target_learners: learners, educators, and AI agents in AI-native education systems
target_learning_goals: cognition-aware interpretation of learner development supporting adaptive intervention
examples: The ECD System (ECDS) prototype interface shows learner portraits, cognition summaries, class-level aggregation views, and AI Twin reasoning panels

article_title: Expert Cognition Dashboard: From Learning Analytics to Cognition Intelligence in AI-Driven Education
citation: Yuan, A. (2026). Expert Cognition Dashboard: From Learning Analytics to Cognition Intelligence in AI-Driven Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.17263
title: Three-level ECD architecture: individual, class, and AI Twin expert dashboards
description: The article proposes a multi-level cognition architecture of three interconnected layers: the Individual Cognition Dashboard (learning portrait, cognition radar, AI Tutor reports), the Class Cognition Dashboard (collective misunderstandings, group tension, cognition heatmaps), and the AI Twin Expert Dashboard (cross-group reasoning, intervention priorities, adaptive planning). Behaviours are "first interpreted through AI Tutor analysis and transformed into cognition structures before being aggregated across individual, class, and AI Twin levels."
requirements: AI Tutor interpretation layer producing cognition reports as foundational inputs for aggregation
constraints: The AI Twin does not observe raw learner behaviours directly but reasons through aggregated cognition structures
target_learners: individual learners, class groups, and cross-group educational ecosystems
target_learning_goals: multi-level cognition interpretation and adaptive educational intervention
examples: The cognition radar visualises conceptual understanding, interpretive consistency, identity confidence, value recognition, and cognitive tension

article_title: Generative AI as a Design Variable: An Evidence-Centered Framework for Principled Governance in STEM Assessment
citation: Gao, Y., Chen, Z., Li, M., & Zhai, X. (2026). Generative AI as a Design Variable: An Evidence-Centered Framework for Principled Governance in STEM Assessment.
title: ECD-based framework treating GenAI as a design variable with three sequential governance stances
description: The framework applies Evidence-Centered Design's three models—student, evidence, and task—as sequential decision criteria for GenAI governance in STEM assessment. It analyzes how GenAI reshapes each model and, as the abstract states, "specifies when to restrict, scaffold, or require GenAI use in STEM assessment." Decisions are organized across two branches (AI interaction competency is or is not the target construct) with a construct revision loop, and the authors note that "Governance decisions are not static" and require ongoing reassessment as capabilities evolve.
requirements: Assessment designers must explicitly specify the target construct, the evidence rules linking work products to it, and the task design before choosing a governance mode
constraints: Decisions may shift as GenAI capabilities and task designs evolve, requiring ongoing reassessment
target_learners: STEM students in higher education, particularly introductory physics
target_learning_goals: Disciplinary competence measured under GenAI integration, including disciplinary AI interaction competency
examples: Figure 1 depicts Branch A (AI interaction competency targeted, leading to Require) and Branch B (not targeted, leading to Scaffold or Restrict decisions) with a grey dashed construct-revision path

article_title: When LLMs Slow Down: How Environmental Impacts Mediate University Students' LLM Usage
citation: Hyeonwook Kim, Xuesi Chen, Alex Cabral, Cindy Kaiying Lin, Udit Gupta, Josiah Hester. (2026). When LLMs Slow Down: How Environmental Impacts Mediate University Students' LLM Usage. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.23968v1
title: Eco-feedback LLM interface with five latency-based eco modes and four sustainability visualizations
description: A live LLM chat interface in which "Users can choose among multiple eco modes, each characterized by a distinct latency profile and corresponding carbon impact based on backend hardware configurations." Eco modes 1–5 trade response latency for lower emissions via tensor parallelism, batching, and renewable energy scheduling, within SLA constraints. The interface adds real-time latency and GHG metrics, cumulative carbon savings, annualized real-world impact equivalents, and a latency–emissions trade-off graph. It was deployed with 89 CS undergraduates in a computing ethics course.
requirements: Operates under Service Level Agreement constraints, managing response latency to balance user experience and carbon emissions
Requires backend configuration knobs (GPU count, batch size, renewable energy scheduling) to realize latency–emission trade-offs
constraints: The study assumed a fixed backend of four GPUs, batch size one, and no renewable energy scheduling, producing coarse-grained latency shifts that do not capture production systems' continuous behavior
Carbon modeling involves uncertainty; the latency–GHG relationship illustrates general trends rather than precise real-world performance
target_learners: undergraduate computer science students
target_learning_goals: awareness of the environmental impacts of everyday LLM use
understanding of latency–carbon trade-offs in AI systems
examples: Participants used the live system over three days across ten sections of a Computer Ethics course, experiencing real eco-mode latency differences revealed through interaction rather than advance explanation

article_title: Reclaiming Epistemic Agency: A Critical Framework for Human-Generative AI Co-Agency in Education
citation: Poudyal, B. (2026). Reclaiming Epistemic Agency: A Critical Framework for Human-Generative AI Co-Agency in Education. https://orcid.org/0000-0002-7210-5480
title: Ecological Co-Agency Framework: relational, regulatory, and pedagogical co-agency bounded by human epistemic accountability
description: The article's central conceptual contribution, developed as a Jaakkola-style 'model' contribution from distributed agency, self-determination theory, self-regulated learning, and technology-integration literature. It treats co-agency as 'the relationship between three interdependent and co-constituted dimensions - relational, regulatory, and pedagogical - within a non-negotiable boundary of human epistemological accountability.' Each dimension is elaborated in Section 4, and the framework is illustrated through an undergraduate literature-review assignment in Section 4.5.
requirements: Transparent description of which tasks are assigned to AI versus students
Ethical co-agency: humans retain primary responsibility and accountability for educational outcomes generated by AI
constraints: The article states there is still no empirical evidence that the framework improves student achievement, equity, or teacher workload

K-12 students and teachers
target_learning_goals: epistemic agency
self-regulated learning
responsible use of generative AI

article_title: Reconceptualizing digital literacy in the AI era: A systematic review of validated frameworks from an ecological perspective
citation: Zemin Guo, Wenhui Li, Laure Lu Chen, Qianru Liang, & Yuxuan Wu. (2026). Reconceptualizing digital literacy in the AI era: A systematic review of validated frameworks from an ecological perspective. Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, 11, 100679. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.caeai.2026.100679
title: Ecological three-level lens (micro, macro, chrono) for analyzing how AI reshapes digital literacy frameworks
description: The review organizes its analysis with Bronfenbrenner's ecological perspective, treating digital literacy as the developmental outcome of interplay between individuals and nested environmental systems across time. It distinguishes three levels: "the micro-level ecologies focus on digital literacy practices situated in school contexts; the macro-level ecologies foreground structural drivers, such as cultural and economic factors, of the digital divide across countries and regions in the AI era; and the chrono-level ecologies trace the conceptual evolution of digital literacy in response to advances in AI." Each level anchors one research question of the review.
requirements: Requires framing digital literacy as emerging from individual–environment interplay across nested systems rather than as an individual trait alone
constraints: The review applies the lens to school-context digital literacy frameworks published January 2014 to February 2025
target_learners: students and citizens in school settings
educators including teachers and school leaders
target_learning_goals: digital literacy development
AI literacy development
digital citizenship
examples: The review's three research questions respectively address micro-level commonalities across frameworks, macro-level differences across socio-economic regions, and chrono-level AI influences

citation: M.M. Chiu, B.W.Y. Chow, C. McBride, S.T. Mol. (2016). Students’ sense of belonging at school in 41 countries: cross-cultural variability. Journal of Cross-Cultural Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1177/0022022115617031

article_title: Enhancing Student Competency Models for Game-Based Learning with a Hybrid Stealth Assessment Framework
citation: Henderson, N., Kumaran, V., Min, W., Mott, B., Wu, Z., Boulden, D., Lord, T., Reichsman, F., Dorsey, C., Wiebe, E., & Lester, J. (2020). Enhancing Student Competency Models for Game-Based Learning with a Hybrid Stealth Assessment Framework. Proceedings of The 13th International Conference on Educational Data Mining (EDM 2020), 92-103. https://educationaldatamining.org/EDM2020/proceedings/
title: Evidence-Centered Design (ECD) as the methodological foundation for stealth assessment in game-based learning environments
description: Evidence-centered design is a systematic approach for designing knowledge assessments in terms of evidentiary arguments, featuring three core models: a task model defining the activities students undertake, an evidence model that processes low-level action sequences into machine-interpretable evidence, and a competency model that dynamically estimates student mastery. In this article, ECD grounds the stealth assessment framework in Geniventure, where the task model consists of "60 challenges across six game levels," the evidence model links gameplay behaviors to targeted genetics concepts, and the competency model estimates mastery of 16 concepts aligned to post-test scores. Stealth assessment conducts real-time processing of data from these three models to inform adaptive scaffolding without disrupting gameplay.
requirements: Validated post-test assessment aligned to the ECD competency model to provide ground-truth competency labels for model training
constraints: Open-ended post-test items must be omitted from competency score calculations due to scoring ambiguity
Concepts with zero-variance post-test responses provide no training signal
target_learners: middle school and high school students (ages 11-18)
target_learning_goals: introductory genetics concepts including heredity, dominance and recessive traits, protein-to-trait relationship, breeding, test cross, and complex inheritance patterns
examples: In Geniventure, the task model defines 60 challenges across 6 levels, the evidence model processes timestamped gameplay actions (allele changes, hint requests, answer submissions), and the competency model estimates mastery of 16 genetics concepts from post-test item correctness

article_title: Stealth assessment of creativity in a physics video game
citation: Shute, V. J., & Rahimi, S. (2020). Stealth Assessment of Creativity in a Physics Video Game. Computers in Human Behavior. https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0747563220303940
title: Evidence-centered design (ECD) framework for stealth assessment
description: ECD is a framework for designing assessments as evidentiary arguments, consisting of three main models: a Competency Model defining claims about student competencies, an Evidence Model specifying what behaviors constitute evidence, and a Task Model defining tasks that elicit that evidence. In stealth assessment, ECD formalizes claims about the learner and the evidence supporting them, allowing continuous performance data from complex interactive environments like video games. The article uses ECD to build the creativity assessment in Physics Playground, with game levels serving as tasks.
requirements: Assessment must elicit behavior bearing evidence about key competencies and provide principled interpretations of that evidence

target_learning_goals: creativity (fluency, flexibility, originality)
conceptual physics understanding
examples: In Physics Playground, the competency model has creativity as parent node of fluency, flexibility, and originality; evidence model variables include number of agents drawn and trajectory deviation from expected solutions

article_title: A systematic review of game-based assessment in education in the past decade
citation: Su, F., & Zou, D. (2024). A systematic review of game-based assessment in education in the past decade. Knowledge Management & E-Learning, 16(3), 451–476. https://doi.org/10.34105/j.kmel.2024.16.021
title: Evidence-centered design (ECD) as a conceptual framework for integrating assessments into educational games
description: ECD is a conceptual design framework for crafting educational assessment tests, "emphasizing consistency between the evidence gathered and interpreted and the underlying knowledge addressed by assessments". In game-based environments it guides researchers to collect evidence making valid claims about students' competency levels during gameplay. Researchers employing ECD specify the competences to be assessed, outline corresponding assessment tasks, and collect evidence such as interactions and behaviors during gameplay to infer students' mastery levels. The review reports ECD was the most-cited framework (N = 6) and recommends integrating it when crafting GBAs.
requirements: Researchers identify the competences to be assessed and predicted, decide on the evidence required, and design in-game tasks to collect that evidence
constraints: The review notes only two studies used multiple theories, indicating theory use in GBA is largely unitary
target_learners: K-16 and higher-education learners assessed within educational games
target_learning_goals: Valid inference of learners' in-game competencies from gameplay evidence
examples: Shute et al. (2021) used ECD in Physics Playground, analyzing learners' in-game actions to deduce understanding of qualitative physics; Song and Sparks applied ECD in Seaball, evaluating students' arguments to assess reasoning skills

article_title: Designing and Evaluating Evidence-Centered Design based Conversations for Assessment with LLMs
citation: Diego Zapata-Rivera, Carol Forsyth, Edith Aurora Graf and Yang Jiang. (2024). Designing and Evaluating Evidence-Centered Design based Conversations for Assessment with LLMs. Leveraging Large Language Models for Next Generation Educational Technologies, CEUR Workshop Proceedings. https://ceur-ws.org
title: ECD-based LLM conversation design process with a five-module prompt structure
description: A design framework for building conversation-based assessments with LLMs via prompt engineering, applying Evidence-Centered Design so conversations stay on the domain topic and elicit construct evidence. The prompt comprises five modules: (1) introduction and domain using the persona and audience patterns, e.g. "Your name is John. You are humorous and reliable study partner"; (2) a conversational schema with Socratic questioning, misconception handling, and turn-length limits; (3) persona behavior modeling via negations and response-type handling instructions; (4) restating of the four-step process; and (5) evidence instructions triggering a terminate command and an XML Toulmin evidence diagram aligned to constructs and standards.
requirements: A clear definition of the construct and the behaviors/interactions needed to make claims about student mastery before prompt design
Iterative refinement of prompts, including negations for specific response types, which can result in long prompts that may be difficult to manage
constraints: The mastery score the LLM produces is not yet validated
The approach was developed and illustrated for formative assessment of skills such as science inquiry in a volcano-eruption context

target_learning_goals: science inquiry skills
argumentation
communication skills
examples: A prompt assessing science inquiry in the context of volcano eruptions instructed the LLM to keep turns to 100 words or less and to end the conversation and produce evidence when the student types terminate

Proximal (microsystem) contexts include parenting quality and the home environment; distal (mesosystem) contexts include neighborhood safety; macro contexts include poverty and SES. article_title: An Introduction to Ecological Active Learning
citation: Azzurra Ruggeri. (2022). An Introduction to Ecological Active Learning. Current Directions in Psychological Science. https://doi.org/10.1177/09637214221112114
title: Ecological active-learning framework: learning strategies are adaptive tools matched to environmental structure
description: The article introduces ecological active learning as a developmental framework focusing on children's ability to adapt and tailor active-learning strategies to the structure and characteristics of a learning environment. It builds on bounded and ecological rationality, understanding rationality as a match between a subject's mental abilities and the structure of the environment. Strategies are 'like tools in a toolbox: No strategy is suitable for all problems, just as different tasks call for different tools.' The framework is the first to apply this perspective to the developmental trajectory of information-search strategies across the life span.
requirements: Learners must be able to detect, and potentially actively discover, the structural characteristics of the learning environment in order to adapt their strategies to them
constraints: The framework focuses on adaptiveness rather than effectiveness measured against adults' default performance; effectiveness of strategies cannot be measured in absolute terms but depends on task characteristics, available resources, and the learner's prior knowledge
target_learners: children from infancy through late childhood, with implications across the life span
target_learning_goals: adaptive information search and question asking
exploration and hypothesis testing
examples: The Toma the monster question-asking examples illustrate how constraint seeking suits uniform hypothesis distributions while hypothesis scanning suits skewed distributions

article_title: Ecocultural patterns of family engagement among low-income Latino families of preschool children.
citation: McWayne, C. M., Melzi, G., Limlingan, M. C., & Schick, A. (2016). Ecocultural Patterns of Family Engagement among Low-income Latino Families of Preschool Children. Developmental Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0040343
title: Ecocultural theory and niche profiles as a lens for family engagement
description: Ecocultural theory holds that development is embedded in ecological and cultural environments, examining the interplay between individual processes and socio-contextual conditions. The article states that "ecocultural theory presupposes that families organize daily routines and activities according to cultural values, available economic and social resources, community norms, and specific contextual demands." Families occupy distinct "eco-cultural niche profiles," and everyday routines including family engagement are proposed to mediate children's developmental outcomes. The study uses this lens to identify within-group engagement patterns rather than comparing Latino families to a dominant-group standard.
requirements: Assessment of family behavior must include the family's or culture's own values and goals
constraints: The theory guides comparison away from majority-favoring group contrasts by basing comparisons on specific ecocultural circumstances
target_learners: Low-income Latino preschool children in Head Start programs
target_learning_goals: School readiness: language and social skills foundational to the transition into formal schooling
examples: The study applied the niche-profile concept by running latent profile analyses separately for Spanish- and English-speaking caregivers

article_title: Children's Effortful Control and Academic Achievement: Mediation Through Social Functioning

title: Effortful control as temperamentally based self-regulation grounded in the executive attention network
description: The article frames effortful control as "a group of temperamentally based skills viewed as the basis of self-regulation," defined by Rothbart and Bates as "the efficiency of executive attention—including the ability to inhibit a dominant response and/or to activate a subdominant response, to plan, and to detect errors." Drawing on Posner's attention networks, the study locates EC in the executive attention network, which monitors and resolves conflicts among other neural networks and is hypothesized to play a central role in regulatory efforts. EC is measured via adult reports of attentional and inhibitory control and behaviorally via persistence or delay tasks.

article_title: Do we need teachers as designers of technology enhanced learning?
citation: Kirschner, P. A. (2015). Do we need teachers as designers of technology enhanced learning? Instructional Science, 43, 309–322. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-015-9346-9
title: Ecology of education: learning as a systemic interaction of learners, teachers and tools
description: The article frames education as an ecology in which effective, efficient and enjoyable learning is determined by exchanges between learners, teachers and their tools within and in interaction with the environment. Learners bring prior knowledge, skills, attitudes, dispositions and self-regulation; teacher quality strongly shapes education and educational innovation; and digital tools, virtual environments and physical spaces must integrate seamlessly, in the sense of ubiquitous computing. As a system, education is a complex whole of interconnected elements; as systemic, any change in one part affects all the rest, and the system is bounded yet influenced by its environment (policy, inspectorates, unions, economy).
requirements: Research into teachers as designers of TEL must accommodate the systems and systemic nature of the ecology of education
constraints: The article warns that too much emphasis on TEL and its technology can come at the detriment of learning in general, citing CSCL research that emphasized the computer first
target_learners: teachers
educational researchers
teacher educators
target_learning_goals: designing effective, efficient and enjoyable learning within the whole educational system
examples: The article cites CSCL research that emphasized computer support first and collaboration later, often to the detriment of learning, and the 'new learning' movement that became a goal unto itself

citation: Katherine M. Zinsser, H. Callie Silver, Elyse R. Shenberger, and Velisha Jackson. (2022). A Systematic Review of Early Childhood Exclusionary Discipline. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543211070047
title: Ecological systems theory as the organizing framework for factors associated with early childhood exclusion
description: The review uses Bronfenbrenner's ecological systems theory to structure its synthesis of factors associated with ECCE exclusion, organizing predictors into micro- (child and family characteristics), meso- (teachers and classrooms), and exo-system (program administration, policies, resources) levels. The authors state that "Children's exclusions are the result of a series of adult decisions that themselves are informed by context." They deliberately exclude the macrosystem and chronosystem because those involve contextual factors evolving over extended periods. The framework is used to identify gaps in the literature as blind spots in understanding the phenomenon.
requirements: Studies must report predictors that can be assigned to ecological levels (child, teacher/classroom, program) for the framework to organize findings
constraints: The review does not anticipate identifying research capturing macrosystem or chronosystem phenomena because these evolve over generations
target_learners: children birth to age 5 in early care and education settings
target_learning_goals: reducing exclusionary discipline (suspension and expulsion) of young children from early care and education settings
examples: Table 3 of the review assigns each included study's predictors to micro-, meso-, and exo-system columns, with disagreements resolved by lead-author third coding until consensus

title: Bronfenbrenner's ecological framework as applied to educator wellbeing
description: The review applies Bronfenbrenner's original ecological framework to organise understanding of educator wellbeing, in which "educator wellbeing is determined by six, interrelated factors": the individual educator, microsystem, mesosystem, exosystem, macrosystem and chronosystem. The individual layer covers predisposing factors such as life experiences and temperament; the microsystem covers teacher, student and parent relationships and classroom interactions; the exosystem covers indirect structures such as district procedures; the macrosystem covers political, economic, legal and cultural influences; and the chronosystem covers change across time. The review uses this lens to identify strengths and gaps in the evidence on wellbeing initiatives.
requirements: Application of the framework requires analysis across all six ecological layers, which the review notes has not been extensively analysed
constraints: The review states the influence of the ecological layers on educator wellbeing is not well understood

early childhood educators
pre-service teachers
target_learning_goals: understanding and supporting educator wellbeing as a determinant of teaching quality and student outcomes

citation: Steven J. Howard, Kate L. Lewis, Emma Walter, Irina Verenikina, & Lisa K. Kervin. (2024). title: Classification framework distinguishing global quality, global process quality, quality pedagogical interactions, and quality interactions related to curriculum content
description: The review's organising taxonomy for grouping interaction quality characteristics. Beyond the consensus distinction of structural and process quality, it delineates process quality into ECEC global quality, ECEC process quality, quality pedagogical interactions, and quality interactions related to curriculum content. Quality pedagogical interactions are "further subdivided into four categories: (i) building positive relationships; (ii) routines and structure; (iii) educator–child conversations and questioning; (iv) supporting play". Curriculum-content interactions are subdivided into seven categories including global instructional support, literacy, language, mathematics, science and environment learning, diversity, and educator use of materials/resources. The frame permitted evaluating differential associations of global versus finer-grained indices with child outcomes.
requirements: Studies must report interaction quality measures classifiable into the framework's categories, with interactional-quality domains tabled at subscale level where reported
constraints: The article states there is less agreement on delineations within process quality, that overlap exists between dimensions (e.g. conversations and questioning are essential to each), and that other groupings are possible with potential implications for findings

target_learning_goals: Cognitive-academic outcomes (cognitive and academic) and social-emotional outcomes (prosociality and socio-emotional competence)
examples: Studies using overall ECERS-R ratings were grouped as ECEC global quality; total CLASS-Pre-K as ECEC process quality; the CLASS-PreK Emotional Support subscale and ORCE as quality pedagogical interactions; and ECERS-E Literacy, Mathematics, Science and Environment, or Diversity subscales as curriculum-content interactions

description: A conceptual distinction the review describes as guiding ECEC quality research: quality is commonly separated into "distinct yet related process and structural dimensions, rather than conceiving of quality as a unidimensional global construct". Process quality relates to children's interactions with adults and other children and to learning experiences shaped by curricula, resources and materials, whereas structural quality refers to organisational aspects such as adult qualifications, child-to-adult ratios, group size, funding and management. constraints: The review notes some studies instead conceive of global quality indices as meaningful, so the distinction is a dominant but not universal convention

article_title: An ecological approach to understanding transitions and tensions in complex learning contexts
citation: Luke McCrone & Martyn Kingsbury. (2024). An ecological approach to understanding transitions and tensions in complex learning contexts. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00267-1
title: The ecotone concept: transitional zones between learning spaces as a third ecosystem of pedagogic potential
description: The article proposes the ecological concept of the 'ecotone' — a zone of overlap and transition between two ecosystems, translating etymologically to "ecologies in tension" — as a way of thinking about the space between lecture theatre and breakout space. Ecotones are "a distinct third ecosystem subject to conflicting tidal and river forces which create tensions" and, being "less encumbered by the inertia and rules of the adjoining spaces", present opportunities for transition and innovation that feedback into the core. The authors postulate this metaphor may significantly advance understanding of complex interactions between space and pedagogy, and suggest applications to diverse student groups and to 'onlife' hybrid physical-virtual learning spaces.
requirements: Requires an ecological mindset that views formal and informal spaces as interconnected rather than fixed, isolated entities
constraints: The article acknowledges the use of the ecotone concept in higher education is limited and presents challenges in applying a metaphor from nature to model social systems
target_learners: undergraduate and postgraduate university students
lifelong and hybrid learners
target_learning_goals: understanding and enabling transitions between transmission-based and active learning
designing productive learning spaces and timetables
examples: Applying the ecotone metaphor helped recognise the formal and informal spaces as greater than the sum of their parts and facilitated institutional discussion that raised awareness of tensions

title: Ecology of Resources model of context
description: The Ecology of Resources is a specification and a method for modelling a learner's context, developed from the ZAA and ZPA concepts. It is grounded on the definition that a learner has a single context that is their lived experience of the world, a 'phenomenological gestalt' reflecting their interactions with multiple people, artefacts and environments. The role of the More-Able Partner is to work with learners to select the optimal resources from a learner's ZAA, which extends beyond a single piece of software to include peers, home environment and wider school resources. Associated with the model is a design framework with a three-phase process for working with educators to develop context sensitive technologies.

title: Embodied conversational agent Jack for restaurant-context English conversation practice
description: The system is an embodied conversational agent, personified as Jack, implemented with the Unity game engine front-end and Node.js back-end, built on the authors' previous work. It supports spoken dialogues in a restaurant context where learners are welcomed, guided to a table, order drinks and dishes, and request the bill. Jack also uses non-verbal backchannels like gaze, head nods, smiles, and blinking.

article_title: Trends, tensions, and futures of maker education research: a 2025 vision for STEM+ disciplinary and transdisciplinary spaces for learning through making

title: Adopt an ecological lens on maker education rather than a technocentric focus
description: The editors recommend that research and practice treat technologies as tools that mediate cultural practices, skills, and social organizations rather than as the primary focus. They argue that "a technocentric approach with an agenda to promote the use of technology per se... should be de-stressed as the primary focus in future research." Instead, the deliberate integration of specific tools and materials into the overall context of maker activities should be stressed.
requirements: Teachers should not be expected to design maker-oriented learning experiences without support; ample time working with maker technologies and some technical proficiency are necessary before incorporation into lessons
constraints: An overly technocentric approach may lead to a decrease in students' and teachers' interest in making

target_learning_goals: Learning through making and design

article_title: The role of teachers in a sustainable university: from digital competencies to postdigital capabilities
citation: Lina Markauskaite, Lucila Carvalho, Tim Fawns. (2023). The role of teachers in a sustainable university: from digital competencies to postdigital capabilities. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10199-z
title: Ecopedagogies as a macro-level postdigital pedagogy for sustainability
description: Ecopedagogies are education models rooted in transformation-based teaching and critical theory, aimed at ending socio-environmental injustices, including those in the digital infosphere. They invite combinations of multiple perspectives and knowledges (e.g., indigenous and western), ask for a shift from local to planetary perspectives, and involve teachers unpacking hidden assumptions about development and sustainability. The article positions them at the macro (planetary) level of the educational ecosystem, with digital technologies playing a crucial role in enabling connections and knowledge co-creation.
requirements: Teachers and students being open and flexible, searching for the value of multiple perspectives and disciplinary stances
constraints: Teachers must consider not only pedagogical benefits of power-intensive technologies such as videoconferencing and AI but also their consumption of natural resources and environmental impact
target_learners: university teachers
university students
target_learning_goals: critical literacy about sustainability and development
transforming societal structures
examples: The article notes ecopedagogies may include helping students learn when not to use technology or when to find alternatives

description: The article classifies ECE into three modalities defined by authenticity of interaction: real clinical interactions ("Students interact with real patients in authentic clinical settings"), simulated clinical interactions (simulated patients in "controllable, safe and repeatable" environments, e.g. standardised patients, OSCE, manikins), and virtual environment learning (digital interfaces "without direct interaction with a human"). The taxonomy structures the review's inclusion criteria and its subgroup analyses of differential effects by modality.

constraints: The classification rests on authenticity of interaction and task complexity as defined by the authors for dental education contexts

article_title: Impact of emotional competence on clinical reasoning: a scoping review.
citation: Joly Louise, Nunes de Sousa Alexandra, Bardiau Marjorie, Dory Valérie, Bayot Marie, Lenoir Anne-Laure. (2026). Impact of emotional competence on clinical reasoning: a scoping review. BMJ Open. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2025-113483
title: Mikolajczak's five-component emotional competence framework crossed with Young's clinical reasoning categorisation as the review's organising axis
description: The review organises its synthesis around two frameworks. EC is described in Mikolajczak's framework, which "includes five components: emotion identification, regulation, expression, use and understanding", each comprising three levels (knowledge, application ability, natural propensity), distinguishing EC from emotional intelligence. CR is categorised per Young et al into reasoning skills, performance, process, outcome, context and goals of reasoning. The review cross-tabulates EC categories (emotion regulation, identification, empathy, gut feeling, global EC scores) against CR categories (clinical performance inside/outside the operating room, CR development, intuitive reasoning, uncertainty management, prescriptions, patient outcomes) to map links and identify gaps.
requirements: Studies must operationalise EC via Mikolajczak's five components and CR via Young's categorisation to fall within the review's scope
constraints: The review excluded articles on emotions' impact on well-being, students' academic success independent of CR, psychiatric disorders, and instrument-handling skills only
target_learners: physicians
medical students
residents
target_learning_goals: clinical reasoning
diagnostic and therapeutic decision-making
uncertainty management
emotional competence
examples: The review's Table 4 cross-tabulates EC categories against CR categories with the methodology type of each linked study, and Table 2 reports frequencies such as 59 articles on emotional regulation strategies and 23 on uncertainty management.

article_title: Comparing a Program Implemented under the Constraints of an RCT and in the Wild
citation: Newman, D., Lazarev, V., & Zacamy, J. (2016). Comparing a Program Implemented Under the Constraints of an RCT and in the Wild. SREE Spring 2016 Conference. https://www.sree.org
title: Ecological validity of RCTs as a threat arising from the experimental design itself
description: The article frames ecological validity specifically as the effect of the experimental design itself, rather than as a generic kind of external validity. It argues that an experiment's validity is threatened when controls or processes required for internal or external validity cause the program to deviate from how it would run outside the experiment, citing Gibson's perception studies and Cole and colleagues' critique of laboratory cognitive psychology. The authors use this framing to ask whether recruiting, training, supporting, randomizing, and measuring for the RCT positively or negatively affect outcomes, and to motivate comparing RCT treatment schools with Scale-up schools implementing the same program.
requirements: Comparable data must be collectable from participants inside the RCT treatment group and from participants implementing the same program outside the trial, ideally in comparable schools
constraints: In this study a direct comparison of school achievement was not possible because the RCT used a researcher-administered outcome measure, so the approach relied on teacher self-report and correlational characteristics
target_learners: high school teachers and students in content-literacy programs
target_learning_goals: discipline-specific literacy and learning in content areas
examples: The study compared 11 RCT treatment schools with 31 Scale-up schools in one state, all trained in the same summer institutes, using teacher and principal surveys and a participant tracker.

citation: Ning, Zhuang, Wen, Xu, Wang, Peng, Huang and Tian. (2025). Evaluating ECAMM-based training efficacy for malaria microscopists in Hunan Province, China. Frontiers in Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpubh.2025.1598917
title: ECAMM framework for external competency assessment of malaria microscopists
description: The WHO External Competency Assessment of Malaria Microscopists (ECAMM) framework is a standardized assessment and training structure for malaria diagnostic competency. It "employs standardized test panels comprising 20 negative slides, 20 positive slides (single/mixed infections at defined parasite densities)" plus falciparum-positive thick/thin smears for quantification, with slides verified by Level 1-certified experts and molecular diagnostics. This article adapted ECAMM into a condensed 4-day training prioritizing diagnostic accuracy over parasite quantification for post-elimination settings.
requirements: Slides verified by ECAMM Level 1-certified experts and molecular diagnostics; participants complete examinations within a strictly enforced 10-min window per slide.
constraints: The 24-participant cohort exceeded ECAMM's recommended cohort size of 12, which the authors say increased logistical challenges; future iterations will adopt smaller cohorts.
Parasite quantification training was provided but not formally assessed because baseline skill levels precluded quantification assessment.
target_learners: public health laboratory microscopists in CDC institutions
semi-skilled personnel in post-elimination malaria settings
target_learning_goals: accurate qualitative identification of malaria-positive and negative blood smears
Plasmodium species differentiation
examples: The Hunan pilot integrated ECAMM core modules through didactic lectures, four 105-min standardized slide-reading assessments, group reviews of misdiagnosed slides, and structured participant surveys over 4 days.

citation: Gelmann D, Giordano J, Gaillard J, Bryant C. (2025). Cardiac Arrest: An Adult eCPR Simulation Case. MedEdPORTAL. https://doi.org/10.15766/mep_2374-8265.11521
title: Low-cost eCPR cannulation manikin built from a CPR trainer torso with fluid reservoir and gel-mold legs
description: The article describes a custom manikin for practicing ultrasound-guided ECMO cannulation: "a Little Anne Laerdal CPR trainer torso with the internal pieces removed and inserted a fluid reservoir with connected tubing coursing through legs made of gel molds". It supports vascular access with real cannulae and ultrasound guidance, and its total production cost was $500 with a cost breakdown in Appendix A. It was used in six simulation sessions and is presented as easily replicable without 3D printing.

constraints: The article notes a prior published protocol required three-dimensional printing, a resource not available at all institutions; this manikin was designed to avoid that dependency

Critical care fellows
Nurses, pharmacists, respiratory therapists, and advanced practice providers
target_learning_goals: Perform ultrasound-guided percutaneous groin cannulation for ECMO via modified Seldinger technique
examples: Used in six simulation sessions, each with four to six participants, in a simulated ED resuscitation bay

title: Monthly 1-hour interprofessional ECMO initiation simulation training with roles, resuscitation scenario, and debriefing
description: A recurring clinical education program at Keck Medicine of USC in which trainees attend a single 1-hour simulation focused on "the interprofessional collaboration and decision-making needed to evaluate a patient for the initiation of ECMO therapy." Participants are assigned roles of primary physician, code blue response provider, and cardiac surgeon, work through a cardiac arrest scenario with relative ECMO contraindications, perform a moderate-fidelity mock cannulation, and finish with a postsimulation debriefing facilitated by simulation faculty. interprofessional clinical team members (nursing, respiratory therapy, anesthesia)

decision-making about ECMO candidacy and initiation
technical skills such as cannulation and resuscitation procedures

article_title: Inconsistencies in rater-based assessments mainly affect borderline candidates: but using simple heuristics might improve pass-fail decisions.
citation: Schauber, S. K., Olsen, A. O., Werner, E. L., & Magelssen, M. (2024). Inconsistencies in rater-based assessments mainly affect borderline candidates: but using simple heuristics might improve pass-fail decisions. Advances in Health Sciences Education, 29(5), 1749–1767. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10459-024-10328-0
title: Ecological rationality as a framework for rater-based assessment decision making
description: The article adopts the framework of ecological rationality, from research on heuristic decision making, as a theoretical lens on rater-based assessment. The framework holds that "even simple decision rules—heuristics—can boost decision making greatly, especially in realistic, uncertain contexts", and that fast and simple rules can outperform complex approaches when they fit the context, making them ecologically rational. The authors apply it for the first time to assessment data in health professions education, using it both to explain examiner discrepancies and to motivate simple decision rules for resolving them.
requirements: Decision rules must fit the decision context to be ecologically rational, as the article states heuristics outperform complex approaches only given that they fit the context
constraints: The framework had, per the authors, never before been applied to assessment research in health professions education, so practical implications should be considered with care
target_learners: Medical students assessed in rater-based performance examinations
target_learning_goals: Accurate and defensible pass-fail decisions about candidate performance
examples: The study applied follow-the-most-experienced, follow-the-most-confident, and decision-tree rules to examiner-pair judgments of mock oral-exam videos

title: Video-viewing test of a simulated patient for assessing empathic communication (ECS-V)
description: An assessment instrument in which participants watch an approximately 5-minute video of a simulated patient interviewed by a midwife and are asked what they would say to her verbatim; responses are rated on the EUIP 5-point empathy scale by expert raters. The article presents it as akin to a mock interview but "more standardised and easier to quantify", and as more convenient and cost effective than OSCEs, which require staff and time. Interrater agreement on 20% of responses was κ = 0.80.

perinatal healthcare workers

article_title: Learning clinical skills: an ecological perspective.
citation: Brymer, E., & Schweitzer, R. D. (2022). Learning clinical skills: an ecological perspective. Advances in Health Sciences Education, 27(3), 691-707. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10459-022-10115-9
title: Ecological dynamics framework for learning clinical skills
description: The article proposes an ecological theoretical rationale for clinical education blending Gibsonian ecological psychology with dynamical systems theory. It holds that "individual and group behaviour is predicated on the person-environment relationship" and that learning emerges through constant interaction of system components rather than through enrichment of internalised representations. Learning design should therefore be built around the learner-environment relationship.
requirements: Learning experiences must be designed with the environment in mind, treating the person-environment relationship as the unit of design rather than isolated mental processes
constraints: The authors present this as an argument and framework applied to clinical psychology contexts; the principles are stated as applicable to clinical training more broadly rather than empirically tested in the article
target_learners: clinical psychology trainees in health settings
target_learning_goals: clinical skills such as forming a therapeutic alliance, assessment and interpersonal effectiveness
examples: The paper contrasts the framework with the Boulder Model scientist-practitioner tradition dating to 1949, and illustrates it with Psychology Clinic supervision and eating-disorder multidisciplinary training

article_title: Emotional and Cognitive Aptitudes and Successful Academic Performance: Using the ECCT.
citation: Vera María; Cortés José A. (2021). Emotional and Cognitive Aptitudes and Successful Academic Performance: Using the ECCT. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health, 18(24), 13184. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph182413184
title: ECCT — Emotional and Cognitive Competence Test
description: The ECCT is a patented admission test (patented in 2015 by Cortés and Vera) used at an Ecuadorian technological institute that measures verbal aptitude, numerical aptitude and abstract reasoning via dichotomous scored items (maximum 90 points), plus emotion regulation through six scored scenarios (0–20) and a 15-item Likert self-questionnaire. The article proposes it as an admissions instrument for Ecuador, analogous to the SAT in the United States. Its CFA fit in this sample was χ2(48) = 124.298, RMSEA = 0.029, CFI = 0.98.
requirements: Administered as the institute's admission test each semester to select students
constraints: AVE for verbal aptitude and the self-questionnaire fell below the 0.50 criterion in this sample
target_learners: higher education students in Ecuador
target_learning_goals: measuring cognitive aptitudes and emotion regulation for admissions and performance prediction
examples: 1750 students sat the ECCT in the first semester of 2018; 1338 enrolled and three semesters of grades were tracked for 796 of them.

article_title: Clinically contextualised ECG interpretation: the impact of prior clinical exposure and case vignettes on ECG diagnostic accuracy.
citation: Viljoen Charle André, Millar Rob Scott, Manning Kathryn, Hoevelmann Julian, Burch Vanessa Celeste. (2021). Clinically contextualised ECG interpretation: the impact of prior clinical exposure and case vignettes on ECG diagnostic accuracy. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-021-02854-x
title: ECG training should not rely on experiential learning alone but be supplemented by formal methods of instruction
description: The article argues that because clinical exposure to ECG conditions is opportunistic and incomplete, experiential learning must be deliberately supplemented. It states that "ECG training should therefore not rely on experiential learning alone, but instead be supplemented by other formal methods of instruction", and proposes that ECG exposure be maximised during clerkships so trainees become familiar with curriculum-specified conditions. This rests on its finding that prior real-patient exposure predicted diagnostic accuracy more strongly than vignettes.
requirements: Exposure opportunities during clerkships must be maximised so trainees encounter the conditions specified by undergraduate and postgraduate ECG curricula
constraints: Generalisability is limited to the undergraduate clerkships and residency programme at the authors' institution and would need study in other contexts
target_learners: Undergraduate medical students
Medical residents
target_learning_goals: ECG interpretation competence for a core syllabus of arrhythmias and waveform abnormalities
examples: The study surveyed 176 trainees on when they last saw each of 25 core ECG conditions during clerkships and found junior students had seen only 52% of them

title: High-fidelity simulation case embedding a certified medical interpreter in an eclamptic-seizure scenario for formative assessment of interpreter use
description: A simulation case in which a 31-year-old Spanish-speaking postpartum woman presents with eclamptic seizures and her Spanish-speaking family member arrives seeking information, so the learner must request and properly use a certified medical interpreter to obtain the history. The article describes it as "a low-stakes, formative simulation assessment tool" with multisource assessment by a faculty observer and the interpreter, checklists, debriefing materials, and appendices including the case script, SP development tool, labs, assessment tools, and debriefing information.
requirements: High-fidelity mannequin, simulation operator, nurse simulated participant, Spanish-speaking actor for the family member, certified Spanish medical interpreter, and faculty evaluator
Briefing and walk-through training for interpreters, simulated participants, and faculty raters before assessment days
constraints: Designed for formative, low-stakes purposes; the authors state high-stakes use would require further validation of scoring and standardized evaluator training
The underlying diagnosis may be too difficult for residents in unrelated specialties

target_learning_goals: Appropriate use of medical interpreter services
Recognition and management of postpartum eclampsia
Communication with a non-English-speaking family member and the health care team
examples: Implemented with 60 emergency medicine residents in fall 2016 as part of a semiannual formative simulation assessment program; each case took approximately 15 minutes and about 20 cases were completed per room per day.

article_title: Online patient simulation training to improve clinical reasoning: a feasibility randomised controlled trial.
citation: Plackett R, Kassianos AP, Kambouri M, et al. (2020). Online patient simulation training to improve clinical reasoning: a feasibility randomised controlled trial. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-020-02168-4
title: eCREST — the electronic Clinical Reasoning Educational Simulation Tool
description: eCREST is an online patient simulation (OPS) in which students watch videos of actors playing patients presenting to their primary care physician with respiratory problems that could indicate serious conditions like lung cancer. "The student gathers information from the patient, while continually being prompted to review their differential diagnosis", then makes a final differential diagnosis and receives feedback after each of three cases. Cases were co-written with real patients who helped identify pertinent clinical and behavioural characteristics. eCREST prompts reflection throughout the consultation and provides feedback enabling reflection on performance afterwards.
requirements: An internet-accessible delivery platform; in cohort two it was integrated into the faculty online learning management platform (e.g. Moodle) to maximise uptake
constraints: Feasibility study only; effectiveness not yet estimated and a summative trial is needed
Acceptability could be affected by faculty-level barriers such as insufficient technological capabilities and lack of alignment of OPS content with educators' needs
target_learners: Final-year undergraduate medical students
target_learning_goals: Clinical reasoning skills
Data gathering from patients
Reducing cognitive biases (unpacking principle, confirmation bias, anchoring)
examples: In the feasibility RCT, the intervention group received three video patient cases in eCREST, all presenting with respiratory or related symptoms to their primary care physician, while the control group received teaching as usual

citation: Terregino Carol A., Copeland H. Liesel, Sarfaty Suzanne C., Lantz-Gefroh Valeri, Hoffmann-Longtin Krista. (2019). title: Empathy and Clarity Rating Scale (ECRS)
description: The ECRS is a communication assessment instrument for medical students comprising seven five-point scale items under four headings (fostering relationship/supporting emotion, gathering information, providing information, helping the patient make decisions). As the article states, "The final ECRS was comprised of seven five-pointscale items," with narrative comments preceding behaviorally anchored ratings where 5 = desired behaviors and 1 = ineffective communication, and intermediate ratings based on the adjustment needed to reach the desired level. It was developed via focus groups, CARE-measure alignment, and modified nominal group processes.
requirements: Raters first write narrative comments on observed behaviors, then assign a rating using the behavioral anchors, considering the learner's level of training
constraints: Content-validity evidence reflects data from a single institution and one year of medical students
Narrative comments may challenge current electronic scoring systems for an OSCE
target_learners: first-year medical students
target_learning_goals: empathetic and clear communication with patients
examples: Used by an actor-trained rater to score 128 archived OSCE encounters and by raters in the improv-experience comparison at RWJMS
